name: Brow thread lift

card.summary: Threads placed to hoist the brow tail without surgery; evidence is thin, with one trial on durability just registered.
card.note: No published trial results found; durability is the open question.

quick.overview:
A brow thread lift uses threads under the skin to raise the outer part of the eyebrow, offered as a less invasive alternative to a surgical brow lift.
No completed trials exist. A registered study is planned to test how long the effect lasts.
quick.mechanism: Threads are anchored in the brow and forehead tissue to hold the brow tail higher. Surgical lifts instead reposition tissue through incisions, and botulinum toxin raises the brow by relaxing opposing muscles [1].
quick.risks: Specific complication rates for brow threads were not found. Brow lifts in general carry risks such as infection, bleeding and numbness [1].

lead: A brow thread lift is a minimally invasive procedure in which threads are placed under the skin to suspend and raise the tail of the eyebrow. People choose it to lift a drooping or low-set brow tail, which opens up the eye area and gives a more alert, youthful look, without the incisions of a surgical brow lift. [1][2]

It sits between injectables and surgery. Wikipedia describes surgical brow lifts, with types including endoscopic, coronal and direct approaches, and non-surgical options such as botulinum toxin, which many patients repeat every four to six months. [1] Thread lifts more broadly use barbed sutures to pull facial skin upward without removing skin. [3]

Eyebrow position matters to appearance because the brow is central to expression: Wikipedia notes that eyebrows evolved as a primary means of communication, and that cosmetic changes to them, from shaping to tattooing to lifting, have followed fashion across history.[2] Brow-lift surgery is often described as a way to give a more youthful or, in some cases, more feminine look, and people interested in the eye area discuss thread suspension as a lower-downtime option.[2]

Published evidence is limited. One registered trial, not yet recruiting as of its listing, plans to examine whether upper blepharoplasty with ligament release improves the durability of thread-assisted brow suspension. [4] A case report has described a vascular complication after a thread brow lift. [5]

chain: Threads anchored in brow and forehead tissue
Brow tail held in a higher position
More open eye area and lifted look
angle.text: The thread suspension repositions the outer brow upward, which people use to lift a heavy or low brow tail and brighten the eye area without a scalp or forehead incision.

infobox: One registered trial, not yet recruiting [4]
Arteriovenous fistula of superficial temporal vessels (case report) [5]

paras: Thread-assisted brow suspension uses sutures or threads to hold the brow in a higher position without the incisions of an endoscopic or coronal lift. Surgical brow lifts, by comparison, include endoscopic lifts through small incisions, coronal lifts across the scalp, and direct, mid-forehead, pretrichial, temporal and internal approaches. [1]

The brow sits at the centre of the upper face: the eyebrow carries expression, and its position and shape have been modified cosmetically across history, from hikimayu in Japan to tattooing in the twenty-first century. [2] Brow lifting was first described in the medical literature in the early twentieth century; Wikipedia credits German surgeon Erich Lexer with a 1910 discussion on forehead lifts. [1]

Wikipedia's thread lift article describes thread lifts as using silicone threads with barbs to pull facial and neck skin upward without removing skin, sometimes marketed as a non-surgical facelift, with variants such as the APTOS technique and the suggestion that combining threads with other rejuvenation methods can improve results.[3] The same article states that the threads are non-absorbable in the version it describes, so complications can be permanent.[3]

The earliest description of brow lifting in the medical literature is credited by Wikipedia's eyebrow article to French surgeon Raymond Passot in 1919, while its forehead-lift article credits Erich Lexer with a 1910 discussion; brows can also be affected during face lifts and eye lifts.[2][1] Botulinum-toxin injection to raise the brow by relaxing opposing muscles began in the 1970s according to the eyebrow article.[2]

Eyebrow fashion has varied widely: Japanese hikimayu practised from the eighth century involved shaving or plucking brows and painting higher ones on the forehead, Elizabethan women of status removed brows altogether, thin plucked brows were fashionable in the 1920s and 1930s, and eyebrow tattooing (microblading) became popular in the twenty-first century.[2] Other options include brow transplant, in which follicles taken from the scalp are implanted, and pencils, gels and powders that make brows look fuller.[2]

Botulinum toxin injections can raise the brow temporarily and are repeated every four to six months. [1] Absorbable Endotine implants have been used in surgical lifts, though they may not support very thick forehead tissue or heavy brows. [1]

Endoscopic brow lift uses three to five incisions of about 3/8 inch and a lighted camera; the coronal lift uses a long scalp incision and was popular in the 1980s and 1990s but has become less common than the endoscopic approach; other methods include direct, mid-forehead, pretrichial, temporal and transblepharoplasty lifts.[1] Since Botox became widespread, many consumers have chosen injections every four to six months instead of surgery for a similar effect, and Botox is also used after some lifts.[1]

Surgical brow lifts are described as having rare, usually minor complications in trained hands, including numbness, hair loss or hairline change, infection and bleeding. [1] Thread lifts in general can leave threads in the skin, so problems can be hard to reverse; a physician quoted by the BBC called thread lifts among the more hazardous aesthetic procedures, and a BBC investigation of a training course reported poor infection control. [3]
A 2023 case report described an arteriovenous fistula of the superficial temporal vessels after a thread brow lift. [5]

Wikipedia's thread lift article quotes a cosmetic doctor describing the thread lift as the most dangerous procedure an aesthetic practitioner can perform, notes that UK aesthetic practitioners are not required to hold mandatory qualifications, and reports a BBC investigation in which an undercover nurse found poor infection control, punctured blood vessels and patients who had drunk alcohol on a training course in Liverpool; the BBC found 26 training academies offering courses priced from 150 to 5,000 pounds in 2021.[3] A MACS lift has been used to correct complications from an APTOS thread lift.[3]

For surgical brow lifts, Wikipedia reports that surgeons switch from endoscopic to open technique in about one percent of cases, that hairline brow lifts have the highest revision rates, direct brow lifts most often cause numbness, endoscopic lifts are most associated with hair loss, and coronal lifts carry higher risk of raising the hairline and reducing scalp sensation.[1]

A registered interventional trial (NCT07879456) with a planned 90 participants will assess durability of thread-assisted brow suspension combined with ligament release during upper blepharoplasty, in people with brow ptosis and dermatochalasis; it is listed as not yet recruiting. [4] No results are available. Published human data otherwise consist of case reports. [5]

timeline.event: Hikimayu, shaving and repainting higher eyebrows, is practised in Japan.[2]
Erich Lexer writes the first documented medical discussion of a forehead lift, according to Wikipedia.[1]
French surgeon Raymond Passot publishes the earliest description of brow lifting in the literature, per the eyebrow article.[2]
Doctors begin injecting botulinum toxin into brows to raise them.[2]
Coronal brow lift is popular before endoscopic lifts take over.[1]
BBC investigates cosmetic training academies in Liverpool, including thread-lift courses.[3]
Case report describes an arteriovenous fistula after a thread brow lift.[5]

lore.intro: Community discussion of thread brow lifts was not found in the material reviewed; the procedure appears mainly in clinic and medical contexts.

claims.claim: A thread brow lift raises the brow tail without surgery.
claims.believers: Clinics and patients describe threads as a lower-downtime way to lift a heavy or low brow tail compared with endoscopic or coronal surgery.[3]
claims.experts: No completed trial of thread brow suspension was found; a registered trial (NCT07879456) plans to test durability when combined with ligament release.[4]

claims.claim: Thread lifts are an easy alternative to Botox.
claims.believers: Patients seeking a longer-lasting effect than the four-to-six-month interval of injectables consider threads.[1]
claims.experts: A doctor quoted by Wikipedia and the BBC calls thread lifts among the more hazardous aesthetic procedures, and a case report describes a vascular complication after a thread brow lift.[3][5]
